title: OpenAI
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in OpenAI coding interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates commonly describe from OpenAI technical interviews: transactional key-value stores, versioned snapshots, in-memory filesystems, caches (LRU and LFU), lazy iterators, rate limiters, task schedulers, expression evaluation, and interval coverage.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can warm up on clean parsing and range checks before building multi-part stateful data structures.
- The selection is approximate. Interview prompts evolve and vary by team, so treat this track as practical systems-in-the-small practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates often report practical, multi-part stateful design prompts (such as an in-memory KV store with transactions, versioned snapshots, or a custom cache/scheduler) where follow-ups add nested transactions, expiration, or stricter complexity bounds.
- Clean invariants, well-factored helper methods, defensive handling of edge cases (empty scopes, missing keys, boundary timestamps), and clear complexity trade-offs are commonly emphasized.
- Follow-ups frequently test whether your data structures remain O(1) or O(log n) under heavy update/query mixes.

How to prepare
- State the invariants between your backing data structures (for example, map + doubly linked list, or scope stack + tombstones) before writing code.
- Handle deletion and rollback carefully: distinguish between a missing key and a key deleted inside an active transaction or version.
- Walk through nested or boundary cases (nested rollback, zero-capacity cache, empty nested iterators) before declaring a solution done.
